summary: In the early 1830s Mexico's government tried to slow the flood of settlers from the United States into Texas, then part of the state of Coahuila y Texas: a law of 1830 banned further American immigration and new imports of enslaved people. When Antonio López de Santa Anna abandoned the federal Constitution of 1824 and concentrated power in Mexico City, Anglo-American settlers and many Tejanos rose in revolt. Fighting began at Gonzales on 2 October 1835, and by December Texian volunteers had driven the last Mexican garrison out of San Antonio de Béxar. Early in 1836 Santa Anna led an army north. His troops stormed the Alamo on 6 March, while General José de Urrea swept up the coast and some 350 Texian prisoners were executed at Goliad. A convention declared independence on 2 March. Sam Houston's army retreated east, then routed Santa Anna at San Jacinto on 21 April 1836 and captured him the next day. The Treaties of Velasco promised a Mexican withdrawal, but Mexico refused to recognise the Republic of Texas.
casualties: An estimated 600 Texian and 1,000 Mexican soldiers died in the fighting and executions of 1835–36, with about 350 Texians and 400 Mexicans wounded and some 700 Mexican soldiers captured.

brief.hook: When Santa Anna tore up Mexico's federal constitution and tightened his grip on Texas, its American settlers and many Tejanos took up arms.

sides.who: Anglo-American settlers, Tejano federalists and volunteers from the United States, who declared the Republic of Texas in March 1836
Mexico's centralist government under President Santa Anna, its garrisons in Texas and the army he marched north in 1836

brief.resultLine: Houston routed Santa Anna at San Jacinto on 21 April 1836; the captured president signed the Treaties of Velasco, but Mexico refused to recognise Texan independence.

strategies.name: No quarter
strategies.text: Santa Anna treated foreign volunteers as pirates and took few prisoners. Nearly all the Alamo's defenders died, and about 350 men who had surrendered were shot at Goliad.

strategies.name: Houston's retreat
strategies.text: Houston fell back east with civilians fleeing alongside, drilling his small army while critics fumed. Captured couriers finally showed him where Santa Anna was, with only part of his divided army.

strategies.name: Surprise at San Jacinto
strategies.text: About 900 Texians charged the Mexican camp during the afternoon rest and overran it in some eighteen minutes. About 630 Mexicans were killed and 730 captured; nine Texians died.

impact: Texas lived as an independent republic for nearly ten years, until the United States annexed it in 1845.
Annexation, and a dispute over the new state's border, led directly to the Mexican–American War of 1846–48.
Through that war, Texas and much of today's American Southwest passed from Mexico to the United States.

details: Tension had been rising as Santa Anna's government turned against federalism, and in September 1835 General Martín Perfecto de Cos landed at Copano with about 500 soldiers. Troops from San Antonio de Béxar were sent to take back a small cannon lent to the settlers of Gonzales for defence. The settlers refused to give it up, and on 2 October 1835 Texian volunteers attacked Lieutenant Francisco de Castañeda's dragoons, who withdrew to Béxar after a brief skirmish. The clash began open war.

Presidio La Bahía at Goliad guarded the road between the coast and San Antonio and held supplies the Mexican army needed. On 10 October 1835 about 125 Texian volunteers under George Collingsworth stormed it and took the small garrison after a fight of about half an hour. The loss cut Cos off from the port of Copano. The next day the volunteers gathered at Gonzales elected Stephen F. Austin to command their army, which then marched on San Antonio.

As the Texian army advanced on San Antonio de Béxar, where Cos had gathered his troops, about 90 men under James Bowie and James Fannin camped by Mission Concepción. On 28 October 1835 Colonel Domingo Ugartechea attacked them with about 275 infantry and cavalry and two cannon. Sheltered along a riverbank, the Texians beat back the attacks and lost one man killed, while Mexican dead are estimated at 14 to 76. The Texians then settled down to besiege Béxar.

Delegates from the Texas settlements met at San Felipe de Austin on 3 November 1835 to decide what they were fighting for. Most still hoped to restore Mexico's federal Constitution of 1824 rather than break away. The Consultation set up a provisional government with a governor and a council, created a regular army and on 13 November named Sam Houston its commander-in-chief. Quarrels between governor and council soon left Texas with weak and divided leadership.

During the siege of Béxar, Texian scouts reported a Mexican pack train approaching the town on 26 November 1835, and many believed it carried silver to pay Cos's troops. Edward Burleson's men attacked and drove the escort back into the town, killing an estimated 50 Mexican soldiers for two Texians wounded. The mules turned out to be carrying fodder for the garrison's horses, and the skirmish became known as the Grass Fight. The siege dragged on into December.

After weeks of siege, Ben Milam and Frank Johnson led volunteers into San Antonio de Béxar on 5 December 1835, fighting from house to house for four days; Milam was killed on 7 December. On 9 December Cos withdrew into the Alamo mission and asked for terms, agreed early on 10 December. His men pledged not to oppose the Constitution of 1824, and Cos left Béxar on 14 December with about 800 soldiers, leaving no Mexican garrison in Texas.

Many volunteers had arrived from the United States, among them the New Orleans Greys, and Mexico's government believed the revolt was being fed from across the border. At Santa Anna's urging, a decree issued in late December 1835 and known after the war minister José María Tornel declared that armed foreigners taken fighting Mexican troops would be treated as pirates and could be executed. It would be invoked to justify the killing of prisoners in the spring of 1836.

Determined to crush the revolt himself, Santa Anna gathered an army of several thousand men at Saltillo and marched it north through a harsh winter. His main force crossed the Rio Grande in mid-February 1836 and made for San Antonio, while General José de Urrea led a second column up the coast from Matamoros. The Texians were poorly prepared: their government was paralysed by quarrels, and many volunteers had gone off to join a planned expedition against Matamoros.

On 23 February 1836 about 1,500 Mexican soldiers entered San Antonio de Béxar, and the town's small Texian garrison under William B. Travis and James Bowie fell back into the fortified Alamo mission. On 24 February Travis wrote his famous appeal 'To the People of Texas & All Americans in the World', pledging to hold out and asking for reinforcements. Few came. Mexican artillery bombarded the walls while more of Santa Anna's troops arrived, and the siege lasted thirteen days.

Advancing up the coast, Urrea's column surprised Frank Johnson's men at San Patricio on 27 February 1836; six Texians escaped and the rest were killed or captured. On 2 March Mexican dragoons ambushed James Grant's party at Agua Dulce Creek, killing twelve, Grant among them. Both groups were what remained of the planned expedition against Matamoros, which had pulled men and supplies away from San Antonio and Goliad. Urrea's victories opened the coastal road to Goliad.

While the Alamo was under siege, an elected convention met at Washington-on-the-Brazos on 1 March 1836. The next day it adopted a declaration of independence proclaiming the Republic of Texas and accusing Santa Anna's government of abandoning the federal constitution. The delegates went on to write a constitution, adopted on 17 March, and chose David G. Burnet as interim president. Sam Houston was confirmed as commander of all Texian forces and left to take charge of the army.

Before dawn on 6 March 1836 Mexican columns stormed the Alamo from several sides and, after their first attacks were thrown back, broke into the compound. Within about an hour nearly all of the roughly 182 to 257 defenders were dead, including Travis, Bowie and Davy Crockett; a handful who surrendered were executed on Santa Anna's orders. Mexican losses are estimated at 400 to 600 killed and wounded. Susanna Dickinson, her infant daughter and Travis's enslaved servant Joe were spared and sent to Gonzales.

Sam Houston had reached Gonzales to gather an army when the survivors of the Alamo brought news of its fall. Around midnight on 13 March 1836 the Texian force evacuated the town, burning whatever it could not carry, and retreated east. Settlers fled ahead of the Mexican advance along flooded rivers and muddy roads, in what became known as the Runaway Scrape. Volunteers kept arriving, and by 19 March about 1,400 men had joined Houston's army.

Ordered by Houston to abandon Goliad and fall back, James Fannin delayed and set out only on 19 March 1836. Urrea's troops caught his roughly 300 men on open prairie near Coleto Creek. The Texians held off attacks through the day, losing about nine killed and 51 wounded against some 50 Mexican dead and 140 wounded. Short of water and surrounded, Fannin surrendered on 20 March, believing his men would be treated as prisoners of war, and they were marched back to Goliad.

Fannin's men and other captured Texians were held at Presidio La Bahía. Urrea appealed for clemency, but Santa Anna, citing the decree on foreign volunteers, ordered them executed, and the commander at Goliad, José Nicolás de la Portilla, obeyed. On Palm Sunday, 27 March 1836, the prisoners were marched out and shot: about 350 by the most common count, with some estimates higher. Twenty-eight escaped and others were spared to work as doctors or labourers. 'Remember Goliad' became a Texian rallying cry.

Houston retreated to the Brazos and drilled his army at Groce's Landing before marching east. Santa Anna, hoping to seize the Texian government, pushed ahead with part of his army and reached Harrisburg in mid-April 1836, but the interim government had fled, and he ordered the town burned. Learning on 18 April that Santa Anna's force was small and close by, Houston hurried toward Lynch's Ferry on Buffalo Bayou, arriving on the morning of 20 April.

Santa Anna camped beside the San Jacinto River, reinforced by Cos to about 1,200–1,360 men. At about 4:30 in the afternoon of 21 April 1836, roughly 900 Texians attacked across open ground shouting 'Remember the Alamo! Remember Goliad!' The Mexican line broke in about 18 minutes, and the killing went on as Texians shot men trying to surrender. About 650 Mexicans were killed and some 300 captured; the Texians lost 11 dead and about 30 wounded, Houston among them.

Santa Anna escaped the battlefield and hid in the marshes, wearing a private's uniform jacket. Texian search parties captured him on 22 April 1836 and brought him before the wounded Houston. Held as a prisoner, he agreed to order the remaining Mexican forces in Texas, under Vicente Filisola and Urrea, to withdraw. Although those armies were still larger than Houston's, they began pulling back toward the Rio Grande.

At Velasco on 14 May 1836 Santa Anna, still a prisoner, signed two agreements with interim president David G. Burnet. The public treaty ended hostilities and required Mexican troops to withdraw beyond the Rio Grande, exchange prisoners and return captured property, including enslaved people. A secret treaty bound Santa Anna to work for recognition of Texas with a border no farther south than the Rio Grande. Mexico's government disowned both, and did not recognise Texan independence until 1848.
